node-1.label: Patient presented with acute shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain, with significant breathlessness on minimal exertion

node-2.label: 30-year-old woman, never-smoker, with medical history of seropositive non-erosive condition diagnosed in 2014; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide level 261 units·mL−1 and rheumatoid factor 30 IU·mL−1

node-3.label: Previous treatments included hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate for three years until 2017, then leflunomide until 2019; certolizumab was added in 2019 and had been used for 18 months at presentation

node-4.label: Physical examination showed normal pulse, normal blood pressure, normal respiratory rate, and normal oxygen saturations on air at rest, but significant breathlessness on minimal exertion (walking a few steps)

why.why: The laboratory physician reports that CTPA shows no pulmonary embolism and that acute PE can be essentially excluded. Despite the initial clinical picture being compatible with PE, this definitive imaging result markedly reduces confidence from 0.35 to 0.05.

Biopsy showing necrobiotic granulomas with pleural extension, absent fever, and the radiologist's assessment that infection is less likely all argue against respiratory infection/pneumonia. Immunosuppression and cavitary lesions still warrant vigilance, but no microbiological evidence supports infection; confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.1.

The biopsy evidence of necrobiotic granulomas with pleural extension shifts the differential away from the less specific pleuritis/ILD category toward necrobiotic nodules. Although RA-associated pulmonary involvement remains likely, the radiologist explicitly favors necrobiotic nodules rather than classic RA-ILD, so confidence in this broad hypothesis is reduced from 0.42 to 0.25.

Biopsy showing necrobiotic granulomas with pleural extension is not typical of drug-induced lung toxicity, and the radiologist judges drug toxicity less likely given the histology and absent fever. No acute temporal trigger has been identified; confidence is reduced from 0.1 to 0.05.

node-10.label: Chest CT shows bilateral small pneumothorax

node-11.label: Chest CT shows cavitary lesions in the lungs

node-12.label: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated necrobiotic nodules (possibly with secondary infection)

why.why: Biopsy showing necrobiotic granulomas with pleural extension, together with negative CTPA, cavitary lesions, bilateral pneumothorax, and absent fever, directly supports rheumatoid necrobiotic nodules as the leading diagnosis. The radiologist's analysis favors necrobiotic nodule-associated pneumothorax over classic RA-ILD, infection, or drug toxicity. Confidence is increased from 0.35 to 0.55, but BAL, HRCT pattern, and PFTs are still pending.

node-13.label: Opportunistic pulmonary infection (e.g., fungal or mycobacterial) complicating immunosuppression

why.why: Histology showing necrobiotic granulomas rather than an infectious organism, plus lack of fever, reduces the likelihood of opportunistic infection. The radiologist explicitly states infection is less likely given the histology and clinical picture; confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.1, with BAL/microbiological studies still pending.

node-14.label: No fever was documented at presentation

node-15.label: Sputum culture/BAL and inflammatory markers are not yet available

node-16.label: HRCT pattern and pulmonary function tests are not yet available
